1: Welcome to Stardust Station. Jax is giving the tour; he's promised not to improvise.
I promised to show you what's here, not what's in the brochure.
I'll join you for the lab portion.
If we get lost, follow the smell of the vending-machine curry. Someone claims it's excellent.
2: This is the main work area. That corner used to be open until we moved the collection bins.
It was necessary to move them *back*. The computer had put one in Noola's turning space.
That's the kind of change I'd rather see than a spotless demonstration.
3: Mira runs the lab. She's prepared a concise demonstration.
It was concise when I started. Then the fourth sample disagreed with the first three.
The disagreeing samples are generally the ones I ask about.
Oh. Then you're going to enjoy this.
It has a very clear set of limits.
And actual photographs. Sorry, I do want you to see the photographs.
4: The material holds under this load and fails above this temperature. Both are repeatable here.
And you don't know what determines where the residue appears?
Correct. We have correlations, not a recipe.
We've refused to collect personal disclosures as explanatory data.
Then I'll judge what you can show me, not what someone wishes you'd measured.
5: These are the original repair logs. Nothing has been edited to make the pilot look tidier.
We didn't put them in the material record.
People told friends things and wrote equipment complaints. Those are not the same permission.
Good. I didn't come here to collect gossip. Though I understand you have excellent dinner parties.
6: You're worried I won't appreciate how much this station does unless it looks exceptional.
I worry you'll see what headquarters sees: small numbers, high costs, and a crew that won't fit neatly in a chart.
I've visited larger sites that looked wonderful until you asked anyone where the spare valves were.
Here everyone can tell you. They might argue about which cupboard first.
7: That low-pressure alarm is real. I need this corridor for a repair.
We've got a visitor standing in the corridor.
A corridor is for getting somewhere. Please use it.
Excellent. Somebody who understands a doorway.
8: We need to turn here. The manifold is ahead and Zib has the service branch isolated.
I know Zib's face. It's the one he makes when somebody wants to walk through the bit he has opened.
Does he often make that face?
Only when he's working. So, quite often.
9: The branch pressure's low. I'll isolate the actuator and check the seal.
I'll take a reading after you shut it down. I won't touch your tools.
Would you rather we move the visitor to the lab?
I'd rather watch how you respond, if we're not in the way.
Stay behind that line and we'll get along famously.
10: Power isolated. Jax, hand me the driver, not the one with the worn tip.
I know which one. You complained about it at Kreeb's dinner.
I'm recording the pressure change, not the social history of your screwdriver.
Access route around the repair is clear.
You all sound like you've done this together before.
The arguing is optional. The competence isn't.
11: Hold the cover while I reseat the actuator.
I have it. Mira, stop trying to take photographs of our hands.
The isolation notice is in place.
And the visitor route stays open at the far end.
I appreciate not being made the most important person in this room.
12: The return is steady. Nothing magical, just a fixed actuator.
You found it and repaired it without waiting for a committee.
Don't say that where Astra can hear you. She'll feel challenged.
13: There's a small residue trace near the warm seam. It may be entirely incidental.
Can you tell me anything useful about it?
Not until I test it. And not if Zib tells me I've left fingerprints on his seal.
You can say you don't know. I wish more scientists would.
I usually have to apologize for saying it.
14: I've seen a narrow material result and a much broader record of real work.
I thought you were here to evaluate the material pilot.
I am. But I can't ignore the people who kept it safe and kept the station running.
That's the part I never know how to put in a box.
15: Our last inspection report was a little unflattering.
Many inspection reports are. The question is whether anyone corrected the problem.
I maintained a separate case file.
It helped me. The station remained mysterious.
16: I'm changing the introduction. The useful record here is the work the crew actually does.
I'm glad. But don't make my sample disappear because it's inconvenient to explain.
I won't. It's a genuine result with genuine limits.
Then we finally have an introduction we can both read without wincing.
17: I can recommend an operating trial based on your maintenance record. The material stays an observation, not a promised output.
That's what we've been trying to tell them.
I can't guarantee central will listen. But I'll put my name on what I saw.
You can thank me after they read the part about costs.
18: We've kept the original field reports, including the ones that went nowhere.
And the crew doesn't have to perform a feeling for the pilot to count.
You can see exactly what we measured.
Good. I'd rather defend an unromantic truth than a very polished fiction.
Even if the unromantic truth comes with several boxes of spare parts?
19: I'll recommend continued operation while central evaluates the actual service record.
That's the first description of this station that sounds like where I work.
I haven't promised you a budget.
I know. I have managed to be disappointed professionally before.
20: That's the correct docking hatch. The other one sticks after a long shift.
I was told I had to be. The brochure is available if you'd like to read a different story.
Do me a favor and don't try the curry on your way out. We have enough reports.
21: The Liaison's recommendation has been submitted.
I didn't expect them to be that reasonable.
They liked the failed tests. I'm choosing to focus on that.
Central review is still pending. Should I keep the celebration cake on hold?
22: They accepted the site and added a material-output target.
To a report that explicitly says we can't predict the output?
Correct. They appear to have read half of it.
That's more than I usually expect, and somehow worse.
